extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecutors/agents as reference)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility analyses (abstract ideas, mental processes, laws/products of nature) including when and how to apply the Step 2A/2B framework and the markedly different characteristics analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental process determination
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation qualifies as a 'mental process' (a type of abstract idea) when the claimed steps can be performed mentally with pen and paper or by human cognition, as reflected in the specification and case law (e.g., CyberSource, Flook, Univ. of Florida Research, Symantec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look to the specification to determine whether the claimed map/analysis/steps are nothing more than a listing or mental procedures performable by humans. Cite cases indicating claimed computations or screening steps can be performed by pencil and paper or mentally. Use the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim is expressed as performed on or requiring a computer, it may nonetheless recite a mental process and thus an abstract idea (e.g., Benson; Mortgage Grader).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must carefully consider the claim's BRI in light of the specification to determine if the invention is described as a concept performed in the human mind and the applicant is merely claiming that concept: (1) performed on a generic computer, (2) performed in a computer environment, or (3) using a computer as a tool. If so, treat the claim as reciting a mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed steps are human cognitive actions merely implemented on general-purpose computer hardware, the claim is directed to an abstract idea (example: Voter Verified; Versata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification describes voting/verifying or pricing determinations as human cognitive actions and the claim only places those actions on a generic computer, the claims may be 'directed to' an abstract idea. Identify whether the computer limitations are generic and do not add a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite mental processes performed in a computer environment (e.g., receiving, screening, distributing email analogous to how a human handles mail) are directed to an abstract idea when nothing in the claim forecloses human performance of the steps (example: Symantec; FairWarning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the specification to compare claimed computer steps to analogous human tasks. If, aside from generic computer-implemented steps, the claims could be performed mentally or with pen and paper, treat as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If the computer is merely a tool that automates mental processes (e.g., anonymous loan shopping, parsing/evaluating data), the claim can be directed to a mental-process abstract idea (examples: Mortgage Grader; Berkheimer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed steps are recited at a high level of generality and merely use computer components as instruments to perform human-performable analysis. If yes, the mental process abstraction applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Both system/product claims (computer system, computer-readable medium) and method/process claims can recite mental processes and thus be directed to abstract ideas (examples: Mortgage Grader, FairWarning, Content Extraction & Transmission).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume only method claims can be abstract ideas. Evaluate system, medium, and method claims equally for mental-process content and apply the same BRI/specification analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative abstract idea procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim limitation does not fall within enumerated groupings of abstract ideas but an examiner believes it should be treated as an abstract idea, it is a 'tentative abstract idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the subject matter eligibility framework: if claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application → Step 2A (NO) → eligible at Pathway B. If not integrated → Step 2A (YES) → Step 2B analysis: if inventive concept present → eligible at Pathway C; if no inventive concept → bring to TC Director attention. A Step 2B rejection based on a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC Director (indicated by form paragraph 7.05.017 and the Director’s signature), and the Office action must justify treating the limitation as an abstract idea. The TC Director will notify Patents Management so the public can be informed (e.g., USPTO website). Examiner may conduct an interview after Step 2B rejection; an interview with the TC Director approving the tentative abstract idea is not required to withdraw or maintain a rejection, though the examiner retains authority to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of nature and natural phenomena — definition and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or lack markedly different characteristics from what occurs in nature. Courts have used terms such as 'physical phenomena', 'scientific principles', 'natural laws', and 'products of nature'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize examples identified by courts (isolated DNA; cloned farm animals; correlations between DNA regions and alleles; metabolic correlations; myeloperoxidase correlations; electromagnetism; bacterial qualities; primers; chemical principles; cell-free fetal DNA; genotype–drug reaction correlations). Use cited case law (e.g., Myriad, Roslin, Merial, Mayo, Cleveland Clinic, O’Reilly v. Morse, Funk Bros., Ambry Genetics, Ariosa, Vanda) when determining whether a claim recites such an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not every claim describing a natural ability/process recites a law of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that describe natural abilities or responses (e.g., cells’ survival, body responses to aspirin) are not necessarily laws of nature; claims focused on process steps applying those natural properties may be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claim is focused on merely observing or detecting a natural ability, or whether it claims process steps that apply or use the natural property (example: Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect — fractionating/recovering/cryopreserving hepatocytes held eligible). Such claims may be eligible at Prong One unless they recite another exception, in which case continue Prong Two (and Step 2B if needed). Manufacturing a new compound by combining components is likewise not per se directed to the components' natural tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting laws/natural phenomena may still be eligible if integrated into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a claim recites a law of nature or natural phenomenon, eligibility can be found if the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application (example: Vanda — tailoring treatment dose to genotype).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such integration is equivalent to finding eligibility at Step 2A Prong Two (Pathway B). Apply Prong Two analysis to determine if the claim applies the natural relationship in a manner that integrates it into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature — scope and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: When a law of nature or natural phenomenon is claimed as a physical product, the exception is often referred to as a 'product of nature'. This includes naturally occurring products and non-naturally occurring products that lack markedly different characteristics from their natural counterparts (examples: isolated DNA, cloned animals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat product-of-nature issues within Step 2A; recognize that synthetically replicated products that are structurally identical to natural counterparts are not patent eligible. Consider the markedly different characteristics analysis to determine whether a claimed nature-based product is a product of nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis (part of Step 2A Prong One) compares claimed nature-based products to naturally occurring counterparts to determine whether the claimed product has 'markedly different characteristics' and thus is not a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these guidelines when a claim recites a nature-based product limitation. If the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics → claim does not recite a product-of-nature exception and is eligible at Pathway B (unless another exception applies). If the entire claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., 'a Lactobacillus bacterium'), once a markedly different characteristic is shown, no further analysis is necessary for eligibility. If the nature-based product does not exhibit markedly different characteristics → claim recites a product-of-nature exception and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two. For claims with additional limitations beyond the nature-based product, also consider whether another judicial exception is recited. Use Chakrabarty and Roslin comparisons as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis should be applied only to nature-based product limitations and not overly extended to whole-claim elements that are not nature-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim includes a nature-based product that is naturally occurring, no need to perform the analysis because the limitation by definition is directed to a naturally occurring product. Do not overextend the analysis to products that, when viewed as a whole, are not nature-based; apply it to each nature-based product limitation to determine whether that limitation is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: BRI considerations and examiner best practices for nature-based product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI), a nature-based product limitation may encompass both eligible and ineligible products; examiners should recognize this when rejecting claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is rejected at Step 2B for failing to provide an inventive concept and the BRI demonstrates the claim covers ineligible embodiments, it is best practice for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment to narrow the claim to embodiments that are not directed to products of nature or that are otherwise eligible. Consider whether the streamlined eligibility analysis (MPEP § 2106.06) is appropriate for inventions that clearly do not seek to tie up judicial exceptions.
